headlines.title: Overtime is the clearest warning sign there is
headlines.detail: 56% of people regularly working overtime left, against 25% of those who did not. Sustained extra hours are not a sign of commitment - they are the sound of somebody burning out.

headlines.title: Junior staff walk, senior staff stay
headlines.detail: 50% of entry-level employees left, against 33% at senior level. Early-career people have the most options and the least tying them to any one employer.

headlines.title: The people leaving are the ones paid least
headlines.detail: Leavers earned ₹76,278 a month on average; those who stayed earned ₹1,25,669 - a gap of ₹49,391 every month. Pay is rarely the whole story, but it is never absent from it.

headlines.title: A stake in the company keeps people in it
headlines.detail: 46% of employees with no equity left, against 26% of those holding even a basic grant. Something that vests over time gives an obvious reason to still be here when it does.

headlines.title: Frequent travellers wear out
headlines.detail: 50% of frequent travellers left, against 0% of those who never travel. Travel is a cost paid in evenings and weekends, and it does not appear on any budget line.

headlines.title: The first two years decide the next ten
headlines.detail: 50% of employees with under two years' service left, falling to 10% past ten years. Get somebody through their second year and they tend to stay for good.

headlines.title: What this costs
headlines.detail: The 18 people who left were earning ₹13,73,000 a month between them. At the standard estimate of 6 months' salary to replace somebody, that is roughly ₹82,38,000 to rebuild the same team you already had.
